heading: Meeting #17 — AI Design Bake-Off (Upcoming)
speakers: None. Hands-on team session led by volunteer team leads.
title: AI Design Bake-Off: Hands-On with AI Design Tools
summary: A hands-on session in which small teams each pick an AI-based front-end design tool and spend about 45 minutes using it to redesign the group's website, cvaiex.org, focusing on look, feel, and user experience. Teams then reconvene to demo their results and compare lessons learned. No coding or design background is required.

heading: Meeting #16 — Breaking Into Data Science & AI Engineering
note: UVA School of Data Science, 1919 Ivy Rd
speakers: Panel: Kerry Guerrero (3E), Hunter Moore (Hardshell AI), Cory Everington (DroneTrace), Patrick Harrison (Data Science Consultant)
title: Breaking Into Data Science & AI Engineering
summary: A joint event with Charlottesville Data Science, in which experienced data scientists, AI engineers, and team leaders shared advice on landing a first or next job in the field. The monthly AI Explorers Book Club met beforehand, and the evening brought the two local communities together for networking.

heading: Meeting #15 — Two For One Talks
speakers: Kyle Carmitchel (CFA Institute; Freehold Software), Justin Schroeder (Braid LLC; Standard Agents)
title: Building a Second Brain / Domain-Specific Agents: Why the Future of AI Is Smaller, Sharper, and Composed
summary: Kyle presented Bosun, a personal agent built with the Claude Agent SDK. It manages his "second brain", connects to email, calendars, and finances, and takes part in family group chats over iMessage. Justin argued for replacing monolithic "Swiss Army knife" agents with small, composable, domain-specific agents that have narrow permissions and clean handoffs, for lower cost, better reliability, and safer deployment.

heading: Meeting #14 — Continuous AI Agents
speakers: John Athayde, Owen Zanzal, Stephen Levin
title: OpenClaw and Other Continuous AI Agents
summary: This meeting focused on persistent AI agents that run continuously and need ongoing operational care. John covered six months of building on OpenClaw, including architecture, refactoring, and operational lessons. Owen walked through installing and evaluating Hermes Agent, and Stephen described using OpenClaw from his phone for social media content and quick code and website updates.

heading: Meeting #13 — Show Us Your Skills
speakers: Mike Powers (opening talk), plus community lightning talks
title: Show Us Your Skills
summary: Mike opened with a 30-minute overview of Agent Skills, an open standard for packaging procedural knowledge and workflows into portable folders. He covered the format, how to build a skill, and the surrounding plugin and marketplace ecosystem. Community members then gave roughly 10-minute lightning talks on skills they had built, adapted, or found useful.

heading: Meeting #12 — Birthday Meetup + AI Security Panel
speakers: Panel of security, cloud, and AI practitioners (panelists not named on the event page)
title: Security in the Age of AI
summary: The group's one-year anniversary meetup, with pizza sponsored by S&P Global, featured a panel on how AI introduces new security risks and amplifies old ones, including prompt injection, data poisoning, and supply-chain vulnerabilities. After a walkthrough of recent real-world incidents, the panel discussed where systems are breaking, what teams get wrong, and whether AI red teams are needed.

heading: Meeting #11 — Demo Day
speakers: Eugene Geis (Bitscopic), Macon Pegram (CapTech), Nish Tahir (Telus Digital), Paul Otto (Teledyne LeCroy), Jill Heinze (Saddle-Stitch Consulting)
title: Demo Day
summary: Five community builders demoed AI projects. Eugene presented PraediVibe, a trust-focused AI analyst that writes clinically accurate SQL over VA healthcare data, and Macon presented a fully local, multimodal photo search engine. Nish showed a model trained to build Magic: The Gathering decks, Paul showed an LLM pipeline for analyzing Bluetooth and Wi-Fi protocol captures, and Jill showed a thinking companion for evaluating risk in AI use cases.

heading: Meeting #10
speakers: Nish Tahir (Principal Applied AI Research Engineer, Telus Digital; formerly WillowTree)
title: Transformers Explained
summary: Nish explained the transformer architecture behind ChatGPT, Claude, Ollama, and Stable Diffusion. His deep dive aimed to build intuition for how these models work without relying on math or jargon.

heading: Meeting #9 — December Meeting
speakers: Eric Pugh (co-founder, OpenSource Connections; OpenSearch project)
title: Tuning the Tuners: Building a Multi-Agent System for Search Relevance Optimization
summary: Eric walked through a multi-agent system he built with the Strands SDK using the "Agents as Tools" pattern, in which an orchestrator agent directs specialized agents to tune search relevance. He demoed the system live and shared lessons on model sensitivity, asynchronous user expectations, and making OpenSearch APIs agent-ready.

heading: Meeting #8 — October Meeting
speakers: Michael J. (MJP) Prichard (Founder & CEO, Shift AI; co-founder of WillowTree and Metis Machine)
title: From Reactive Tools to Proactive Teammates: The Next Shift in AI
summary: A fireside Q&A with one of Charlottesville's serial tech founders on AI moving from command-driven tools to proactive systems that anticipate human intent. Topics included building and funding AI startups in 2025, AI as an amplifier of human creativity, and lessons from scaling multiple companies.

heading: Meeting #7 — September Meeting
speakers: Doug Turnbull (search expert; co-author of *Relevant Search*)
title: What AI Teams Get Wrong about Vector Search
summary: Doug addressed common misconceptions about vector search in RAG and recommendation systems, such as leaning too heavily on embeddings and ignoring established information-retrieval principles. He showed how to combine classical search techniques with modern AI to build vector-driven systems that are practical and reliable.

heading: Virtual Lunch & Learn #1
title: Your README Has a Voice: Turning Repos Into Narrated Onboarding Tools
summary: A practice run of Owen's DevOps Days DC talk about RepoRad.io, an open-source CLI tool that reads a GitHub repo and turns it into narrated audio onboarding episodes using GPT-4 and OpenAI voice synthesis. He covered the architecture, keeping episodes current with GitHub Actions, and the tradeoffs of LLM narration in accuracy, privacy, and tone.

heading: Meeting #6 — August Meeting
speakers: Dan Funk (CEO, SpiffWorks; core contributor to SpiffWorkflow)
title: Transparent AI — Tools and Techniques for Taking the BS out of AI Adoption
summary: Dan showed how SpiffWorks combines BPMN flowcharts and Python into agentic workflows that business leaders and cross-functional teams can read and discuss. The session was a laptop-based lab that took apart how LLMs work, explained them without jargon, and gave attendees ways to teach AI concepts to others.

heading: Meeting #5 — July Meeting (Demo Day)
speakers: Emily Smith (Side Nerd), Michael Pfaffenberger (Walmart), James Kovalenko (nurho.tech)
title: Demo Day
summary: Three community builders gave 20-minute demos. Emily showed Side Nerd, a text-message interface for volunteer tracking built on GPT models and AWS serverless. Michael showed Code Puppy, an AI coding agent that largely wrote itself, and James showed Perseus.tube, an AI-powered tool for searching and analyzing Attic Greek words.

heading: Meeting #4 — June Meeting
speakers: Dylan Isaac (Senior AI Engineer, Deque Systems)
title: Building Ladders: Extending Human Agency with AI
summary: Dylan described his move from accessibility coaching into AI engineering, and how he builds tools that automate drudgery so people can focus on meaningful work. His examples ranged from simple job-simplifying prompts to autonomous agents used in accessibility, development, and personal life.

heading: Meeting #3 — May Meeting
title: From Fuzz to Function: AI for Next-Gen Apps
summary: Justin presented AI as a way to build deterministic, reliable applications from messy human input, not just as a coding assistant. He covered AI routers, prompt chaining, multiplexing, and tool use as techniques for keeping AI systems controllable and predictable.

heading: Meeting #2 — April Meeting
speakers: John Berryman (Arcturus Labs; formerly GitHub Copilot; author of *Prompt Engineering for LLMs*)
title: What is Prompt Engineering?
summary: John explained how user input gets translated into LLM logic, covering data sourcing, prompt assembly, and techniques from zero-shot and few-shot prompting to more advanced methods. The evening also introduced "breakout tracks", member-led side series such as a book club on Chip Huyen's AI Engineering, followed by an open forum.

heading: Meeting #1 — Inaugural Meeting
title: Practical AI in Practice
summary: The kickoff meeting of Cville AI Explorers, a community for building AI skills through hands-on projects, technical sharing, and collaborative learning. Owen gave a short talk on applying AI in practice, followed by an open discussion to shape the group's direction.
